places.name: Jorhat
places.summary: Assam's cultural capital and tea town — 135 gardens, the Tocklai research centre, and the gateway to Majuli.
places.seoTitle: Jorhat — tea gardens and the gateway to Majuli
places.seoDescription: Jorhat, cultural capital of Assam: 135 tea gardens, Thengal Manor, the Tocklai Tea Research Centre and the ferry to Majuli. Best October–April.

images.alt: The namghar at Thengal Manor, Jorhat
images.caption: Thengal Manor, Jorhat

overview.text:
Jorhat is known as the cultural capital of Assam, and it is above all a tea town. Its name comes from "jor hat" — two markets — after the markets that once stood on either bank of the Bhogdoi river. Around the town spread 135 tea gardens, among them Cinnamora, the first tea garden in Assam.

Many estates run guided tours where you can watch the leaf being plucked and learn to taste tea, and some let you stay the night. Thengal Manor, a planter's bungalow built in 1880, shows how the tea families lived. Jorhat is also the jumping-off point for Majuli, the world's largest river island, and for the hoolock gibbons of the Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary. Come between October and April; November brings the Tea Festival.

how_to_reach.text: Fly into Jorhat (Rowriah) airport, which connects with major Indian cities, or take the train to Jorhat Town or Mariani Junction.

best_time.text: October to April is the best time to visit. The Tea Festival is held every November, and Bihu falls three times a year — Magh Bihu in January, Bohag Bihu in April and Kati Bihu in October.

items.body: Tour a tea estate, watch the plucking and learn to taste tea.
See Thengal Manor, an 1880 planter's bungalow.
Visit the Tocklai Tea Research Centre.
Cross to Majuli, the world's largest river island.
Look for hoolock gibbons in the Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary.

where_to_stay.text: Stay on a tea estate — many gardens around Jorhat offer rooms, so you wake up among the tea bushes.

places.name: Tezpur
places.summary: The 'city of eternal love' on the Brahmaputra — ancient ruins, the Agnigarh legend and Nameri National Park nearby.
places.seoTitle: Tezpur — legends, ruins and the Brahmaputra
places.seoDescription: Tezpur on the Brahmaputra: Agnigarh, Bamuni Hills, the Da Parbatia gate and Nameri National Park 35 km away. Best October–April.

images.commons: File:Brahmaputra River sunset from Tezpur, Assam.jpg
images.alt: Sunset over the Brahmaputra at Tezpur
images.caption: The Brahmaputra at Tezpur

overview.text:
Tezpur sits on the banks of the Brahmaputra and calls itself the city of eternal love, after the legend of Princess Usha and Aniruddha, grandson of Krishna. Its old name, Sonitpur — the city of blood — comes from the battle the legend says was fought here.

The history is real too. A nine-line rock inscription of Harjar Varma near the Rudrapada temple dates the city to 829–30 AD; the modern town was founded by the British in 1835. Climb Agnigarh for the river view, see the 9th–10th-century carvings on Bamuni Hills and the Da Parbatia door frame, one of Assam's oldest pieces of sculpture. Nameri National Park, with over 300 bird species, is about 35 km away. Come between October and April.

best_time.text: October to April, when the weather is pleasant for exploring the ruins and the river.

items.body: Climb Agnigarh for views over the Brahmaputra.
See the carvings on Bamuni Hills.
Visit the Da Parbatia door frame.
Go birding in Nameri National Park.

places.name: Dibrugarh
places.summary: The Tea City of India on the upper Brahmaputra — tea estates, Bogibeel Bridge and two great forests nearby.
places.seoTitle: Dibrugarh — the Tea City of India
places.seoDescription: Dibrugarh: tea estate tours, Bogibeel Bridge, Dibru-Saikhowa and Dehing Patkai nearby. Best October–March; airport 15 km from town.

images.commons: File:A view from the bank of the river Brahmaputra in Dibrugarh, Assam.jpg
images.caption: The Brahmaputra at Dibrugarh

overview.text:
Dibrugarh sits on the banks of the Brahmaputra in upper Assam and is known as the Tea City of India. Tea estates stretch out from the town in every direction, and many welcome visitors: walk the rows of bushes, watch the leaf being plucked, follow it through withering, rolling and drying, and finish with a tasting of different grades.

The town is also the base for some of Assam's finest wild places. Dibru-Saikhowa National Park and the rainforest of Dehing Patkai are within reach, and the 4.94 km Bogibeel Bridge, India's longest rail-road bridge, crosses the river nearby. Shop for handwoven gamocha towels before you leave. Come between October and March, when winter days are mild, about 10–25 °C.

how_to_reach.text: Mohanbari (Dibrugarh) airport is about 15 km from the centre, with flights to Delhi, Kolkata and Guwahati; take a taxi or bus into town. Trains arrive at Dibrugarh Town and Dibrugarh Banipur stations.

best_time.text: October to March is best. Winter, November to February, is mild, at about 10–25 °C.

items.body: Handwoven gamocha towels and other handloom.

places.name: Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary
places.summary: The densest rhino population in India, 56 km from Guwahati — an easy day trip for one-horned rhinos.
places.seoTitle: Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary — rhinos near Guwahati
places.seoDescription: Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary, 56 km from Guwahati: India's highest density of one-horned rhinos, plus elephants and buffaloes. Open 7 am–4 pm.

images.commons: File:Baby Indian Rhino at Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary.jpg
images.alt: A young one-horned rhino at Pobitora
images.caption: One-horned rhino, Pobitora

overview.text:
Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary lies just 56 km from Guwahati and has the highest density of greater one-horned rhinoceros in India — even higher than Kaziranga. That makes it the easiest place to see rhinos on a day trip from the city.

The sanctuary was once marshland among paddy fields, protected by local villagers, and became a reserve in 1971. It is named after Pobitora, a daughter of the King of Mayong who died young. Besides the rhinos, nearly 375 species of birds, reptiles and mammals live here, from wild elephants and Asiatic buffaloes to leopards and wild boar. It is open from 7 am to 4 pm, so leave Guwahati early for the best sightings.

places.name: Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra
places.summary: Guwahati's cultural complex for the arts of Assam and the Northeast — 17.5 hectares and over 4,000 artefacts.
places.seoDescription: Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra in Guwahati: a 17.5-hectare cultural complex founded in 1988, with over 4,000 artefacts. Open 10 am–7 pm.

images.alt: Buildings of the Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra
images.caption: Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra

overview.text:
Srimanta Sankardeva Kalakshetra is Guwahati's great cultural complex, named after the poet and playwright Mahapurush Srimanta Sankardeva. Its foundation was laid in 1988 to preserve, promote and present the arts and culture of the people of Assam, and it spreads over 17.5 hectares, with sections devoted to the traditions of Assam and the wider Northeast.

Its collection runs to more than 4,000 artefacts. It is the best single place in the city to get a feel for the region's crafts, dress and stories before heading out to Majuli or Sivasagar. It is open from 10 am to 7 pm. October to April is the pleasant season, with temperatures of about 10–20 °C.

places.name: Madan Kamdev
places.summary: The 'Khajuraho of the East': carved 9th–10th-century temple ruins 40 km from Guwahati.
places.seoTitle: Madan Kamdev — the Khajuraho of the East
places.seoDescription: Madan Kamdev, 40 km from Guwahati: 9th–10th-century Pala temple ruins with carvings of dancers, gods and lovers. Open 9 am–5 pm; best November–February.

images.alt: Carved stone ruins at Madan Kamdev
images.caption: Madan Kamdev

overview.text:
Madan Kamdev is an archaeological site barely 40 km from Guwahati, where the ruins of a temple complex of the 9th and 10th centuries survive. It belonged to the Pala dynasty of Kamarupa, and its carvings — dancing nymphs, gods and goddesses, and lovers — have earned it the name "Khajuraho of the East".

The ruins were described in the 19th century but went unexcavated for decades, and many pieces were lost. Since 1977, when the Archaeological Directorate of Assam took charge, the main temple and the ruins of 12 more temples have been uncovered. Walk slowly among the fallen blocks to find the best carvings. It is open from 9 am to 5 pm; November to February is the best season.

places.name: Chandubi Lake
places.summary: A lake created by the 1897 earthquake at the foot of the Garo Hills — rowing, winter birds and a yearly festival.
places.seoDescription: Chandubi Lake, formed by the 1897 earthquake at the foot of the Garo Hills: rowing, winter migratory birds and the Chandubi Festival. Open 7 am–7 pm.

overview.text:
Chandubi Lake lies at the foot of the Garo Hills in Kamrup district, on the border of Assam and Meghalaya, and it was born of disaster: the great earthquake of 1897 sank the land here and the lake filled the hollow. One local story says the name means "five sinking", for five hills that went under.

Today it is a quiet place, ringed by forest, tea gardens and villages. The water is clear, and migratory birds arrive in winter. You can row or fish on the lake's natural lagoon, and every year the people of Rajapara village hold the Chandubi Festival, with folk music, dances, crafts and Assamese food. It is open from 7 am to 7 pm and makes a peaceful day out from Guwahati.

places.name: Siva Dol
places.summary: The tallest temple in Assam: a 180 ft Ahom Shiva temple of 1734 on the bank of the Sivasagar tank.
places.seoTitle: Siva Dol, Sivasagar — Assam's tallest temple
places.seoDescription: Siva Dol, Sivasagar: built in 1734 by Queen Ambika, 180 ft tall with a golden finial — Assam's tallest temple. Open 6 am–9 pm.

images.alt: The tall spire of Siva Dol beside the Sivasagar tank
images.caption: Siva Dol, Sivasagar

overview.text:
Siva Dol rises 180 feet above the bank of the great Sivasagar tank and is the tallest temple in Assam. It was built in 1734 by Queen Ambika of the Ahom dynasty and remains a living temple, busy with daily worship.

It is a showpiece of Ahom temple architecture. The base measures 195 feet around; the main spire climbs in tiers to a golden finial, flanked by four smaller, identical towers; and the antechamber has a curved roof modelled on the Assamese hut. Inside the sanctum is an unusual reversed Shiva linga. The temple is open from 6 am to 9 pm. Other Ahom monuments are a short ride away.

items.body: Look up at the golden finial on the 180 ft spire.
See the reversed Shiva linga in the sanctum.

places.name: Agnigarh
places.summary: Tezpur's legendary 'fortress of fire' hillock, with sculptures of Usha and Aniruddha and a lookout over the Brahmaputra.
places.seoDescription: Agnigarh in Tezpur: a hillock of legend with sculptures of Usha and Aniruddha and a viewing platform over the Brahmaputra.

images.alt: Sculptures and gardens on Agnigarh hill
images.caption: Agnigarh, Tezpur

overview.text:
Agnigarh — the "fortress of fire" — is a hillock on the bank of the Brahmaputra in Tezpur, and the setting of the town's favourite legend. King Banasura, the story goes, ringed it with a wall of fire and shut his daughter, Princess Usha, inside to keep her from Aniruddha, the grandson of Krishna — a quarrel that ended in a great battle.

Today a circular stairway climbs the hill past stone sculptures that tell the story of the lovers, to a tall viewing platform at the top. From there the Brahmaputra stretches out below you, with the Himalaya on the horizon on clear days. The Mahabhairab Temple, one of Assam's oldest Shiva temples, is a couple of kilometres away.

items.body: Circular stairway to a viewing platform

places.name: Bamuni Hills
places.summary: A hillside of 9th–10th-century carved ruins near Tezpur, with the Da Parbatia gate and its Ganga and Yamuna figures.
places.seoDescription: Bamuni Hills (Usha Pahar), Tezpur: 9th–10th-century temple carvings and the Da Parbatia gate with Ganga and Yamuna. Open sunrise to sunset.

images.alt: Carved stone ruins on Bamuni Hills
images.caption: Bamuni Hills, Tezpur

overview.text:
Bamuni Hills, also called Usha Pahar, is a short drive from the centre of Tezpur and is scattered with the carved remains of temples from the 9th and 10th centuries AD. It feels like an open-air museum: blocks of stone lie across the hillside, many of them covered in fine sculpture.

The best-known piece nearby is the Da Parbatia door frame, one of the oldest surviving examples of temple architecture in India, guarded by the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna. The site is open from sunrise to sunset. Take your time to look closely at the panels, then combine it with Agnigarh, on its hill above the Brahmaputra, and the Mahabhairab Temple for a half day of Tezpur's history.

places.name: Dibru-Saikhowa National Park
places.summary: A river-island park of swamp forest and grassland at the Brahmaputra–Lohit confluence, near Tinsukia — birds, primates and houseboats.
places.seoDescription: Dibru-Saikhowa National Park, 12 km from Tinsukia: 425 sq km of swamp forest and grassland where the Brahmaputra meets the Lohit; birds, primates, houseboats.

images.alt: Grassland and river channels in Dibru-Saikhowa
images.caption: Dibru-Saikhowa National Park

overview.text:
Dibru-Saikhowa National Park lies where the Brahmaputra and the Lohit meet, about 12 km north of Tinsukia, and covers some 425 sq km. It is a watery landscape of salix swamps, tropical and deciduous forest and grassland, laced with river channels, and one of the richest places in Assam for birds.

Migratory and endangered birds draw most visitors, but the park also shelters several primates, from the Assamese and rhesus macaques to the slow loris. Exploring is often by boat, and houseboats and floating hotels let you stay on the water. Add the Maguri-Motapung Beel, a wetland nearby that teems with resident and migratory birds, and the Bogibeel Bridge on the way back to Dibrugarh.

places.name: Dehing Patkai
places.summary: Upper Assam's lowland rainforest — 108 sq km with seven wild cat species, near Digboi and the Stilwell Road.
places.seoDescription: Dehing Patkai: 108 sq km of rainforest, the only reserve in India with seven wild cat species, 293 birds and 301 butterflies; near Digboi.

overview.text:
Dehing Patkai protects 108 sq km of lowland rainforest in upper Assam, dominated by tall hollong, nahar and meloni trees and rich in orchids. It is the only reserve in India home to seven species of wild cat: tiger, leopard, clouded leopard, leopard cat, golden cat, jungle cat and marbled cat.

The numbers are remarkable for its size — 47 species of mammals, 293 of birds, 301 of butterflies and 47 of reptiles — so come for the birds and butterflies as much as for the chance of a cat. History is close by too: the Digboi oil field, discovered in 1889 and one of the oldest in Asia, and the Stilwell or Ledo Road, built in the Second World War to link India with China. The reserve is open all day.

places.name: Bogibeel Bridge
places.summary: India's longest rail-road bridge, 4.94 km over the Brahmaputra at Dibrugarh.
places.seoDescription: Bogibeel Bridge: 4.94 km over the Brahmaputra between Dibrugarh and Dhemaji — India's longest rail-road bridge. Open 24 hours.

images.alt: Bogibeel Bridge stretching across the Brahmaputra
images.caption: Bogibeel Bridge

overview.text:
The Bogibeel Bridge carries both road and railway 4.94 km across the Brahmaputra near Dibrugarh, linking the town with Dhemaji on the north bank. It is the longest rail-road bridge in India, and the view of it striding across the river is one of the sights of upper Assam.

It was built to last: the bridge can stand winds of up to 260 km/h and earthquakes up to magnitude 8.0, and it is an important defence route, carrying troops and supplies towards the border. It is open 24 hours. Drive or take the train across for wide views of the river, or watch it from the bank at sunset. Combine it with a tea-estate visit or a trip to Dibru-Saikhowa.

places.name: Tocklai Tea Research Centre
places.summary: The world's oldest and largest tea research station, in Jorhat — tea museum and garden tours.
places.seoDescription: Tocklai, Jorhat: the world's oldest and largest tea research station, with a tea museum and guided garden tours. Open 8:30 am–5 pm.

images.alt: The gate of the Tocklai Tea Research Centre
images.caption: Tocklai Tea Research Centre

overview.text:
Tocklai, in Jorhat, is the world's oldest and largest tea research station.

The tea museum inside the centre tells the story of tea cultivation through photographs, artefacts and vintage equipment from the industry's early days. You can also join a guided tour of the centre's tea gardens and learn to tell the different tea plants apart. The centre runs training programmes for growers too, on practices such as organic farming. It is open from 8:30 am to 5 pm. Pair it with a visit to one of Jorhat's estates to watch plucking and tasting.

items.body: Browse the tea museum's photographs and vintage equipment.
Join a guided tour of the centre's tea gardens and learn the different tea plants.

places.name: Samaguri Satra
places.summary: Majuli's mask-making satra, keeping the sacred craft alive since the 1600s.
places.seoTitle: Samaguri Satra, Majuli — the mask makers
places.seoDescription: Samaguri Satra on Majuli: the sacred craft of mask-making since the 1600s, and a library of over 200 manuscripts. Open 7 am–5 pm.

images.commons: File:A mask artist of Samaguri Satra, Majuli.jpg
images.alt: A mask maker at work at Samaguri Satra
images.caption: Mask-making, Samaguri Satra

overview.text:
Samaguri Satra is one of Majuli's Vaishnavite monasteries, and it is famous for one thing: masks. Since the 1600s the monks here have kept alive the sacred craft of mask-making, and the satra grew in importance under Sri Sri Chakrapani from 1663.

Visitors can watch the masks being made. Beyond the workshop, the satra's library holds more than 200 ancient manuscripts. Like the other satras, it welcomed people regardless of caste or community. It is open from 7 am to 5 pm, and makes a natural pair with Auniati Satra for Sattriya dance.

items.body: Watch the satra's artists making masks by hand.
Visit the library of over 200 ancient manuscripts.
Combine it with Auniati Satra for Sattriya dance.
